name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,699

clue.text: Satellite state in contest finally awarded bronze

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes inside another
finally points at the end, so only the closing letter of each following word is kept

blocks.note: a game is a contest
NY is the abbreviation for New York State
last letter of awarded
last letter of bronze

explanation.surface: A small client state comes third in some contest and takes the bronze medal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Satellite state' reads as one phrase for a puppet nation, but 'Satellite' alone is the definition. 'finally' works on both 'awarded' and 'bronze'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ganymede is the largest moon of Jupiter, and a moon is a natural satellite orbiting a planet.

clue.text: Chief raised part of ransom in Oregon

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising letters means reading them upwards, back to front
only a portion of the following words is wanted, a run of consecutive letters

blocks.note: the letters running across the end of ransom, all of in, and the start of Oregon

explanation.surface: A tribal leader in Oregon has raised part of a ransom payment.
explanation.walkthrough: Read upward through 'ransOM IN OREGon' to find the name; the Oregon setting points to the American West and its history.
explanation.definitionFit: Geronimo was a famous Apache leader, so he is a chief in the Native American sense of a tribal leader.

clue.text: Wealthy individual with no Scottish coin?

blocks.note: na is the Scots form of no
a bob was the old British shilling coin

explanation.surface: A rich person who, surprisingly, has not a single Scottish coin to their name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scottish' looks as if it describes the coin, but it turns 'no' into its Scots form NA. A bob is slang for the old shilling, a pre-decimal British coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A nabob, originally a returning East India Company fortune-maker, is a person of great riches and conspicuous luxury.

clue.text: Most miserable and possibly least vaccinated

blocks.note: first meaning: most paltry and wretched, the superlative of a contemptible adjective
second meaning, read literally: most covered in a childhood disease spots, as the unvaccinated might be

explanation.surface: A comment about whoever is unhappiest, linking it to having skipped their jabs.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning splits the word as 'most measly', having the worst case of measles, which vaccination prevents; 'possibly' flags the playful logic.
explanation.definitionFit: Measly means contemptibly small or poor, and literally means infected with the spotted viral disease, so the superlative fits both.

clue.text: Live and prosper having nothing set aside

indicators.note: putting aside nothing means a zero-shaped letter is removed and left out

blocks.note: to prosper is to do well
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Echoing the Vulcan salute 'live long and prosper', here with savings spent.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface looks like a two-word phrase; 'Live' alone is the definition and 'prosper' gives the two-word phrase DO WELL.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell somewhere is to reside or make one's home there, a formal synonym for living.

clue.text: Duck circling extremely strange plant

indicators.note: to circle something is to go round it, so one piece surrounds the other
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outermost letters are kept

blocks.note: the teal is a small duck
the first and last letters of strange

explanation.surface: A duck swims round a very odd-looking plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely strange' reads as 'very weird' but means the ends of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: The teasel is a prickly thistle-like herb whose dried heads were once used to raise the nap on cloth.

clue.text: Weird energy harnessed by republic in revolution

indicators.note: something harnessed is held in, so one piece is enclosed by the other
a revolution turns something round, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: Eire is the Irish name for the Republic of Ireland
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A strange force is captured by a country in the middle of an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolution' suggests political upheaval but means turning the republic's name round; the energy then sits just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Eerie describes something strange and unsettling, uncanny in a way that makes the skin prickle.

clue.text: Witness corrupt cop at rest

indicators.note: something corrupt is spoiled or debased, so these letters are put into a broken order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A bent police officer is caught off duty by someone watching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Witness' looks like a verb, telling us to watch the corrupt officer, but it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectator is an onlooker who sees an event happen, just as an eyewitness observes it.

clue.text: Player knocking the block off an American one

indicators.note: the block is slang for the head, so knocking it off removes the first letter

blocks.note: an American player of the flute is a flutist, where Britons say flautist

explanation.surface: A sportsman decapitating an American opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one' refers back to 'Player': an American player of a woodwind instrument, beheaded, becomes a player of a plucked one.
explanation.definitionFit: A lutist is a musician who plays the lute, and a musician performing on an instrument is a player.

clue.text: Composer's time supporting school over in Bonn

indicators.note: in a down clue, a support sits underneath, so this piece goes after the others

blocks.note: SCH is a standard abbreviation for school
über is German for over, and Bonn is a German city
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A composer's career is spent backing a school that has ended up in Bonn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' wants to mean finished or reversed, but 'in Bonn' asks for the German word for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Schubert was an Austrian Romantic composer known for his songs and symphonies.

clue.text: Part of frame CGI bear ruined

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked, so these letters are reduced to a new order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A computer-generated bear spoils part of a film frame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frame' suggests a frame of film, which suits CGI, but here it is the body's frame, the skeleton.
explanation.definitionFit: The ribcage is the bony enclosure of the chest, one section of the skeleton that supports the body.

clue.text: Present scoundrel with what's required by letter

blocks.note: a cur is a contemptible man, originally a mongrel dog
a letter here is someone who lets property, and they require payment from tenants

explanation.surface: Giving a gift to a rogue, along with what a postal letter needs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letter' suggests something posted, needing a stamp; it is a landlord, one who lets.
explanation.definitionFit: Present as an adjective means existing now, and current is a direct synonym for belonging to the present time.

clue.text: Magazine in east Rouen upset prize winners

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one set of letters goes inside another
to upset something is to knock it over, so the letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: Bella is a British weekly women's magazine
the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A magazine in eastern Rouen upsets a set of prize-winners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Magazine' could be a gun part or a store; here it is a specific British title, BELLA, which is then mixed with the other letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Nobel laureates are people awarded a Nobel Prize, the most famous international honours in science, literature and peace.

clue.text: See 12
Some overtime in retirement to get fancy church hat

indicators.note: some of something is only a part, so a run of letters is taken from inside a word
to retire is to withdraw, going back the way one came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the middle letters of overtime

explanation.surface: Working overtime after retiring, someone can afford a fancy hat for church.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'ovERTIMe' backwards. 'retirement' suggests old age, but signals a turnaround.
explanation.definitionFit: A mitre is the tall, ornamented headdress worn by bishops, an elaborate piece of ecclesiastical headgear.

clue.text: Therapy derived from flower involving new team

indicators.note: to involve is to include within, so one piece is wrapped by another
something made new is remade, so these letters take a fresh order

blocks.note: a flower is something that flows, a river; the Trent is a major English river
taken as written

explanation.surface: A herbal therapy made from a flower, now with a fresh team behind it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' is the crossword trick for a river, read as flow-er, not a bloom. The Trent runs through the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Therapy is medical care given to cure illness, and treatment is the general word for such care.

clue.text: Liquid that can be dark but put on pale

definitions.note: a phrase for what gets applied to fencing, standing for the substance

blocks.note: first meaning: a brown or black oily fluid distilled from tar
second meaning: a pale is a wooden fence stake, and this wood preservative is what gets brushed onto fences

explanation.walkthrough: 'pale' looks like the opposite of 'dark', making a colour paradox, but it is the noun for a fence post, as in 'beyond the pale'.
explanation.definitionFit: Creosote is a dark tarry oil distilled from coal tar, painted on fences and timber to stop rot.

clue.text: Code in competition originally replaced by child

indicators.note: originally means at the origin, so only the opening letter is meant
one thing replaced by another is swapped out, so a letter is exchanged

blocks.note: rivalry is competition between parties
the first letter of the rivalry, which is what gets swapped out
CH is a standard abbreviation for child

explanation.surface: A code in a contest was originally swapped for a child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' acts on the competition word found, not on 'competition' itself: its first letter makes way for CH.
explanation.definitionFit: Chivalry was the medieval knightly code of conduct, prizing honour, courage and courtesy.

clue.text: Track workers moving around main glens

indicators.note: things moving around shift position, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Railway workers travel about the principal Scottish valleys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Track' could be a footpath through the glens, but it is a railway track.
explanation.definitionFit: Signalmen operate the railway signals and points from signal boxes, so they work on the railway lines.

clue.text: Sturdy lot with not much up top

blocks.note: having little up top means not bright, stupid
a set is a lot or group

explanation.surface: A sturdy group of people who are short on hair, or brains.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up top' hints at position, but 'not much up top' is an idiom for being dim. The pieces are taken in reverse of their clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: Thickset describes a person heavily and solidly built, stocky and strong, much like sturdy.

clue.text: Put limits on refuse emptied near stern

indicators.note: an emptied word has lost its contents, so only its outside letters remain
near means beside, so the next piece is placed right alongside

blocks.note: the first and last letters of refuse
stern and strict both mean severe

explanation.surface: Limits are put on rubbish being emptied near the back of a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stern' suggests the rear of a boat, fitting refuse being dumped; it is the adjective meaning severe.
explanation.definitionFit: To restrict something is to confine it within bounds, keeping it under control.

clue.text: Measure last of Scotch after some maths backfired

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, the only one kept
something that backfires goes backwards, so the letters run in the opposite direction
after means following, so one piece comes behind another

blocks.note: trig, trigonometry, is a branch of mathematics
the final letter of Scotch

explanation.surface: A measure of the last of the whisky is poured after some calculations went wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measure' suggests a dram of Scotch but is the definition; 'some maths' is one branch of it, not a sum.
explanation.definitionFit: Girth is the measurement around the middle of something, its circumference or waist size.

clue.text: Mimic initially riles copper giving summary

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: to ape is to mimic
the first letter of riles
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: An impersonator annoys a policeman by giving a summary of events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' wants to be a police officer, fitting the mimic who riles; it is the metal, by its chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: An aperçu, borrowed from French, is a brief outline or quick insightful survey of a subject.

clue.text: US singers making modest sums

blocks.note: Tom Petty was an American rock singer
Johnny Cash was an American country singer

explanation.surface: American singers earning only small amounts of money.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'singers' covers two surnames, one for each word of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Petty cash is the small fund of money an office keeps for minor everyday expenses.

clue.text: Produce from Year One regularly peeled

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: Y is the abbreviation for year
I is the Roman numeral for one
the second, fourth and sixth letters of peeled

explanation.surface: Fruit and vegetables grown by Year One pupils, routinely peeled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Year One' reads as a school class, but splits into two abbreviations. 'Produce' is a noun in the surface and the definition alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A yield is the amount a farm or crop gives, the harvest, so it matches produce as a noun.

clue.text: Covering hospital admission of boxer?

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs
a boxer might confess 'I jab', a jab being a quick straight punch

explanation.surface: A covering needed when a boxer is admitted to hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'admission' suggests being admitted to a ward; it is a confession, the boxer owning up to what they do. The question mark flags this playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A hijab is the headscarf worn by many Muslim women, a garment that covers the hair and neck.

clue.text: Finch's tail clipped twice somewhere upstairs

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its end, and clipping it twice trims two closing letters

blocks.note: Atticus Finch is the lawyer hero of To Kill a Mockingbird

explanation.surface: A small bird has its tail feathers trimmed twice and lives somewhere upstairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finch' wants to be a bird, fitting 'tail'; it is a surname, and the first name of its most famous bearer is the one shortened.
explanation.definitionFit: An attic is the room or space directly under the roof, at the top of a house.

clue.text: Letter from those who were kept in reserve

blocks.note: those people, taken as the definite article: the ones in question
the Territorial Army, the British Army's part-time volunteer reserve force

explanation.surface: A message written by people who were held back in reserve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' suggests correspondence, but it is an alphabet letter. The TA was Britain's part-time army reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth letter of the Greek alphabet, used for the th sound.

clue.text: Animal came by 'orse, we're told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the answer matches a spoken phrase

blocks.note: to come here on horseback is to ride here, said with the dropped h of 'orse

explanation.surface: A Cockney-sounding report that an animal arrived on horseback.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in ''orse' tells you to drop every h, so 'rode here' becomes 'rode 'ere'.
explanation.definitionFit: The roe deer is a small Eurasian deer, a wild animal common in British woodland.

clue.text: Clothing those declaring 1 Down

definitions.note: a mass noun standing for the plural garments

blocks.note: first meaning: knitted pullovers, the British word for sweaters
second meaning: parachutists, who traditionally shout the Apache chief's name as they leap

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to the war cry shouted by paratroopers leaping from aircraft; a jumper is also British for a sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: Woollen pullovers are knitwear garments, and people who leap from planes or heights are those who leap.

clue.text: Disordered hammering of DIY nut

indicators.note: hammering something beats it out of shape, so these letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A home-improvement enthusiast bangs away in a chaotic manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nut' suggests the hardware that goes with hammering, but here it means an enthusiast; DIY is do-it-yourself home repair.
explanation.definitionFit: Untidy means messy and lacking order, just as something disordered is jumbled and not arranged.

clue.text: Rich poet almost on a roll

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
in an across clue, one thing on another comes after it

blocks.note: taken as written
a bun is a bread roll
Dante Alighieri was the Italian poet of the Divine Comedy

explanation.surface: A wealthy poet who is nearly on a winning streak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on a roll' is an idiom for doing well, but here it splits: 'a roll' is bread, and the poet sits on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Abundant means plentiful or existing in large quantities, as in land rich in natural resources.
